transitivity: both — transitive (synchronize the files), intransitive (the two clocks synchronize)
gloss: To make two or more things happen or move at exactly the same time.
examples: Let's *synchronize* our watches before we split up.
The dancers *synchronized* their steps perfectly.
The app is *synchronizing* your photos with the cloud.
contrast: American English spells it *synchronize*; the *-ise* form (*synchronise*) is British.

gloss: To sell a column, cartoon, or television show to many newspapers or stations at once.
examples: The network plans to *syndicate* the show next fall.
They *syndicated* the comic strip nationwide in 1994.
Her column is *syndicated* in more than two hundred papers.
contrast: The verb ends in a full vowel — SIN-duh-kayt — but the noun *a syndicate* ends in a schwa: SIN-duh-kuht.

gloss: To organize something into an orderly, consistent system.
examples: The new director wants to *systematize* hiring.
They *systematized* the filing system last spring.
Once the records had been *systematized*, a search took seconds.

gloss: To arrange figures or facts in a table so that they can be compared.
examples: Volunteers *tabulate* the results overnight.
The clerk *tabulated* the votes twice.
We are still *tabulating* the survey answers.

transitivity: both — transitive (she tacked the notice to the door), intransitive (the boat tacked into the wind)
gloss: To fasten something in place with small nails or pins, or to change direction the way a sailboat does.
examples: *Tack* the poster to the bulletin board.
He *tacked* the schedule above his desk.
The campaign has been *tacking* toward the center all month.

gloss: To follow someone closely and secretly in order to watch what they do.
examples: Two agents *tail* him everywhere he goes.
A reporter *tailed* the senator for a week.
She realized she was being *tailed*.

gloss: To spoil the quality or the reputation of something by contact with something bad.
examples: One bad batch can *taint* a whole brand.
The scandal *tainted* his legacy for good.
The water was *tainted* with lead.

transitivity: both — transitive (the wind tangled her hair), intransitive (these cords tangle easily)
gloss: To twist things together into a knotted mess that is hard to separate.
examples: These headphones *tangle* in my pocket every single time.
The wind *tangled* her hair on the way to school.
The kite string got *tangled* in the branches.

transitivity: both — transitive (he tanked the interview), intransitive (the stock tanked)
gloss: To fail or drop in value suddenly and badly.
examples: If the deal falls through, the shares will *tank*.
The movie *tanked* at the box office.
Sales have been *tanking* since the spring.

gloss: To tease someone by showing or promising something desirable that stays out of reach.
examples: Don't *tantalize* the dog with food he isn't allowed to have.
The smell of fresh bread *tantalized* the waiting crowd.
The offer was *tantalizing* enough to make her think twice.

gloss: To give someone a particular job or duty to carry out.
examples: The mayor will *task* a small committee with the review.
They *tasked* her with rewriting the entire manual.
He has been *tasked* to report back by Friday.
contrast: Usually passive, with *with*: *be tasked with doing something*.

gloss: To mark the skin permanently with a design made with needles and ink.
examples: He wants to *tattoo* a compass on his forearm.
She *tattooed* her daughter's name on her wrist.
Both of his arms are heavily *tattooed*.

gloss: To move unsteadily back and forth as if about to fall.
examples: The vase *teeters* on the edge of the shelf.
The company *teetered* on the brink of bankruptcy.
He was *teetering* on a ladder with a can of paint.
contrast: Almost always used with *on*: *teeter on the edge/brink of something*.

gloss: To grow one's first teeth, as a baby does.
examples: Babies usually start to *teethe* at around six months.
She *teethed* early and slept badly for weeks.
The baby is *teething*, so he chews on everything.
contrast: The *th* here is voiced, as in *breathe*; the noun *teeth* ends in a hissing, voiceless *th*.

gloss: To work from home by computer and phone instead of traveling to an office.
examples: Half the staff *telecommute* three days a week.
He *telecommuted* from Denver for all of last year.
*Telecommuting* saved her two hours of driving a day.

gloss: To show what you are about to do before you do it, usually without meaning to.
examples: Good boxers never *telegraph* a punch.
His nervous glance *telegraphed* the answer.
The studio has been *telegraphing* the ending in every trailer.

transitivity: both — transitive (telephone the office), intransitive (she telephoned to cancel)
gloss: To speak to someone by phone.
examples: Please *telephone* the office before nine.
She *telephoned* twice and got no answer.
He is *telephoning* the hotel right now.
contrast: In everyday American English *call* is far more common; *telephone* as a verb sounds formal or old-fashioned.

transitivity: both — transitive (the machine teleports objects), intransitive (the character teleports across the map)
gloss: To move instantly from one place to another without crossing the distance in between.
examples: In this game you can *teleport* back to base.
The crew was *teleported* down to the planet.
He kept *teleporting* behind me and winning the round.

gloss: To make something less harsh or extreme by adding a moderating influence.
examples: Try to *temper* your criticism with a little praise.
Experience *tempered* his early optimism.
Her joy was *tempered* by worry about the cost.

gloss: To offer or present something formally, such as a resignation or a payment.
examples: He plans to *tender* his resignation on Monday.
She *tendered* an apology in writing.
Payment must be *tendered* in full at the counter.

gloss: To make meat softer by pounding it or soaking it in a marinade.
examples: A little acid will *tenderize* the beef.
He *tenderized* the steak with a mallet.
The chicken had been *tenderized* in buttermilk overnight.

transitivity: both — transitive (he tensed his shoulders), intransitive (she tensed at the sound)
gloss: To tighten your muscles or go suddenly rigid, usually out of fear or effort.
examples: Try not to *tense* your shoulders when you lift.
She *tensed* the moment he said her name.
He could feel his jaw *tensing*.

gloss: To call something by a particular name or description.
examples: Economists *term* this a soft landing.
The judge *termed* the delay unacceptable.
What is loosely *termed* artificial intelligence covers many things.
contrast: It takes two objects with no *as*: *they termed the plan a failure*, not *termed the plan as a failure*.

transitivity: both — transitive (she testified that she saw him), intransitive (he testified at the trial)
gloss: To give evidence as a witness, usually in court and under oath.
examples: Three neighbors will *testify* for the defense.
She *testified* that she had never met the man.
He is *testifying* before the committee today.
contrast: The *-y* changes to *-ie-*: *testifies*, *testified*.

gloss: To feel a strong, urgent desire for something.
examples: Readers *thirst* for any detail about the case.
He *thirsted* for revenge for years.
A generation *thirsting* for change filled the square.
contrast: Takes *for*: *thirst for knowledge*, never *thirst something*.

transitivity: both — transitive (they thrashed the home team), intransitive (the fish thrashed in the net)
gloss: To beat someone soundly, or to move about violently and wildly.
examples: They usually *thrash* us on our own field.
The swimmer *thrashed* at the water in panic.
A shark was *thrashing* in the shallows.
contrast: A verb ending in *-sh* adds *-es*: *he thrashes*.

transitivity: both — transitive (fans thronged the square), intransitive (crowds thronged to the gates)
gloss: To gather in or fill a place in a large crowd.
examples: Tourists *throng* the plaza every August.
Thousands *thronged* the cathedral for the service.
Shoppers were *thronging* the sidewalks by noon.

gloss: To choke someone by the throat, or to deliberately limit the speed or flow of something.
examples: Some carriers *throttle* your data after twenty gigabytes.
The provider *throttled* the connection at peak hours.
Video kept freezing because the network was *throttling* traffic.

ru: глухо стучать, ударяться с глухим звуком
gloss: To hit something with a dull, heavy sound.
examples: Boxes *thud* onto the conveyor belt all day long.
The book *thudded* to the floor.
Her heart was *thudding* in her chest.
contrast: The final *d* doubles: *thudded*, *thudding*.

gloss: To turn or handle pages with your thumb; also, to get a free ride by signaling with your thumb.
examples: Don't *thumb* the pages with wet hands.
She *thumbed* a ride all the way to Flagstaff.
He was *thumbing* the index, looking for my name.
contrast: The *b* is silent: THUM.

transitivity: both — transitive (he thumped the table), intransitive (her heart thumped)
gloss: To hit or beat something heavily, making a dull sound.
examples: He *thumps* the table whenever he gets angry.
My heart *thumped* so loudly I could hear it.
Someone was *thumping* on the door at midnight.

gloss: To make the short, sharp sound a clock makes as it marks each second.
examples: You can hear the old clock *tick* from the hallway.
The meter *ticked* while we argued about the fare.
A bomb was *ticking* somewhere in the building.
contrast: In American English you *check* a box on a form; *tick a box* is British.

gloss: To give something a slight trace of a color or a feeling.
examples: A drop of beet juice will *tinge* the icing pink.
Her relief was *tinged* with guilt.
The sunrise was *tingeing* the clouds orange.
contrast: The *-ing* form usually keeps the *e* to protect the soft *g*: *tingeing*.

gloss: To make small changes to something in an attempt to repair or improve it.
examples: He likes to *tinker* with old radios on weekends.
Congress *tinkered* with the formula again.
She spent all Sunday *tinkering* with the engine.
contrast: Takes *with*: *tinker with something*.

gloss: To make a light, high ringing sound, like a small bell.
examples: The bells over the door *tinkle* whenever someone comes in.
Ice *tinkled* in the tall glass.
A piano was *tinkling* in the next room.

gloss: To work long and hard at something exhausting.
examples: They *toil* in the fields from dawn to dusk.
She *toiled* for years over the manuscript.
Crews were *toiling* through the night to clear the road.

transitivity: both — transitive (the sexton tolled the bell), intransitive (the bells tolled at noon)
gloss: To ring a bell slowly and repeatedly, especially to mark a death or an hour.
examples: The church bells *toll* every evening at six.
The bell *tolled* nine times for the fallen.
A single bell was *tolling* as the procession passed.

gloss: To deliberately set something on fire.
examples: Rioters threatened to *torch* the building.
Someone *torched* two cars overnight.
The warehouse had been *torched* for the insurance money.
contrast: In American English a *torch* is a burning stick or a blowtorch; the battery-powered kind is a *flashlight*.

gloss: To destroy something with a torpedo, or to deliberately ruin a plan or an agreement.
examples: A single senator could *torpedo* the whole bill.
A submarine *torpedoed* the tanker.
The talks were *torpedoed* by a leaked memo.
contrast: The third-person form adds *-es*: *he torpedoes it*.

transitivity: both — transitive (don't touch the screen), intransitive (their hands touched)
gloss: To put a hand or another part of the body on something, or to come into contact with it.
examples: Please don't *touch* the paintings.
Her letter *touched* him deeply.
The plane's wheels were barely *touching* the runway.
contrast: A verb ending in *-ch* adds *-es*: *she touches*.

transitivity: both — transitive (the state toughened its laws), intransitive (his hands toughened over the summer)
gloss: To make something stronger or stricter, or to become so.
examples: Lawmakers want to *toughen* the penalties.
The city *toughened* its rules on short-term rentals.
Years at sea had *toughened* his hands.

gloss: To praise something publicly and repeatedly in order to promote it.
examples: Officials *tout* the project as a model for the region.
He *touted* his experience in every interview.
The drug was widely *touted* as a breakthrough.

gloss: To rise much higher than the things around it.
examples: The cranes *tower* over the old harbor.
He *towered* above his classmates by eighth grade.
A stack of files was *towering* on her desk.
contrast: Takes *over* or *above*: *tower over the crowd*.

ru: играть (с мыслью), забавляться; вертеть в руках
gloss: To consider an idea casually, or to handle something idly without real attention.
examples: I *toy* with the idea of moving every winter.
She *toyed* with her food and said nothing.
He has been *toying* with the notion of retiring early.
contrast: Takes *with*: *toy with an idea*.

gloss: To register a name, logo, or phrase legally so that only you may use it.
examples: They tried to *trademark* the phrase "game day".
The company *trademarked* the shape of the bottle.
The slogan is *trademarked* in forty countries.

gloss: To walk or wander about in a tired, aimless, or irritating way.
examples: I'm not going to *traipse* across town in this rain.
We *traipsed* through three museums in one afternoon.
Kids kept *traipsing* through the kitchen in muddy boots.

gloss: To give a drug that makes a person or an animal calm or unconscious.
examples: Rangers had to *tranquilize* the bear.
The horse was *tranquilized* before the flight.
They are *tranquilizing* the elephant so they can move her.
contrast: American English uses one *l*: *tranquilize*, *tranquilized*; British English writes *tranquillise*.

transitivity: both — transitive (transact business), intransitive (most customers transact online)
gloss: To carry out business or an exchange of money with someone.
examples: Most customers now *transact* entirely online.
The firm *transacted* millions in trades that morning.
Business was *transacted* in three languages.

gloss: To go beyond the usual limits of something.
examples: Great music can *transcend* language.
Her appeal *transcended* party lines.
The issue has long since *transcended* local politics.

gloss: To hold someone's attention so completely that they cannot move or look away.
examples: The final scene will *transfix* you.
The verdict *transfixed* the courtroom.
The children stood *transfixed* by the fire.

transitivity: both — transitive (transgress the rules), intransitive (those who transgress are punished)
gloss: To break a rule, a law, or a moral boundary.
examples: Artists like to *transgress* the usual boundaries.
He knew he had *transgressed* an unwritten rule.
Anyone *transgressing* the policy will be suspended.

gloss: To happen, or to become known after having been secret.
examples: No one knows what will *transpire* at the hearing.
It later *transpired* that the email had been deleted.
Nothing of interest has *transpired* since Monday.

gloss: To cause someone lasting emotional shock or injury.
examples: Don't let one bad teacher *traumatize* you.
The crash *traumatized* everyone on board.
He was *traumatized* by what he saw during the flood.

gloss: To travel or move across an area, especially a large or difficult one.
examples: The trail *traverses* three states.
They *traversed* the glacier in two days.
A new bridge *traversing* the canyon opens in May.

transitivity: both — transitive (they trawled the archives), intransitive (the boats trawl for shrimp)
gloss: To search through a large quantity of material for what you want, or to fish by dragging a net.
examples: Investigators *trawl* social media for leads.
She *trawled* the archives for his letters.
Two boats were *trawling* just off the coast.

gloss: To become widely talked about online, or to move steadily in a general direction.
examples: Anything about the finale will *trend* by morning.
The hashtag *trended* worldwide for two days.
Prices have been *trending* downward since March.

ru: определять методом триангуляции; сопоставлять (данные из разных источников)
transitivity: both — transitive (police triangulated his location), intransitive (the candidate triangulates between the two camps)
gloss: To locate a position or establish the truth by combining measurements or sources taken from different angles.
examples: Two towers are enough to *triangulate* a phone.
Police *triangulated* the signal to a motel outside town.
We are *triangulating* the estimates against census data.

gloss: To treat someone or something without the seriousness they deserve.
examples: She is not a woman to *trifle* with.
He *trifled* with her feelings for a year.
You are *trifling* with a very dangerous man.
contrast: Takes *with*, and is heard most often in the negative: *not to be trifled with*.
